I’ve farmed the same 10 mu in Quzhou County for over forty years, and at sixty I don’t see any reason to gamble on something new. My family depends on this land, so I’m sticking to the wheat-maize double crop that everyone around here grows — it’s the only system I trust to put food on the table and leave me with grain to sell. This year I’ll plant winter wheat on all 10 mu in mid-October. I’ll buy improved wheat seed from the village supply store; I tried saving my own seed once about ten years ago and the yield was poor, so I learned my lesson. For the soil, I’ll rotary till before planting — that’s what I’ve always done, and it gets the field ready in a day. I’ll put down about 20 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus 8 kg of phosphorus and 5 kg of potassium. I thought about cutting the fertilizer back to save money because my son sent less cash home from the city this year, but two years ago Old Wang down the road used less nitrogen and his wheat turned yellow at jointing; he lost nearly a hundred jin per mu. I’d rather spend the money than risk that. I’ll irrigate the wheat four times — overwinter, at jointing, and twice more if the spring stays dry — because the pump costs a lot but dry wheat is a disaster.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I have less than a week to get the maize in the ground, so I won’t bother tilling. I’ll plant hybrid maize seed no-till straight into the wheat stubble; that’s what my nephew does on his business farm and it works fine. The maize will get about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium. I’ll irrigate it twice and spray pesticide twice — once for weeds and once for the borers that always show up in August. I won’t hire any labor if I can help it; my wife and I can manage the spraying and watering, though it means long days. I expect around 450 kg per mu from the wheat and about 500 kg per mu from the maize — that’s roughly what I’ve gotten the last few years when the weather cooperates.
